title: Ajahn Funn: Moreover, we come to make merit and wholesome qualities, to do good deeds, so that we receive happiness and ease. When our mind…
content:
When Everyone Has Virtue and Dhamma, Evil Dissolves by Itself Like Darkness Before Fire

Moreover, we come to make merit and wholesome qualities, to do good deeds, so that we receive happiness and ease. When our mind receives happiness and ease, then there are no issues, no problems. Our country becomes peaceful and calm. This is why you must learn to reach the heart and understand. If we are good, even if others are not good – all people, every single one, even the tiny red ant or the little insect – all want goodness. Those who behave badly, who do evil, cannot survive. It is because of this goodness that things are that way. Now, anyone who tries to destroy a good person will themselves be ruined – the destroyer himself. When in our country everyone has virtue and Dhamma, everyone has merit and wholesomeness, everyone is happy, the mind happy and at ease, then evil will dissolve by itself. It is like lighting a fire: the darkness disappears on its own. Those wrong-doers who bring other countries to destroy us – the earth will swallow them up. Just watch. We have taken the Buddha as our refuge. If we go taking other things as refuge and recollection, and just keep trying to revolt and force each other, will it work? Anyone who persecutes the Buddha – the earth really swallows them. So it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: Our saṅkhārā (conditioned formations) are passing away every day, every moment, every minute. What can we take as a refuge? Contemplate so that…
content:
Saṅkhārā Are Passing Away Every Day – What Can We Take as a Refuge?

Our saṅkhārā (conditioned formations) are passing away every day, every moment, every minute. What can we take as a refuge? Contemplate so that you know and see. Your own refuge – the reason we all have come here is because we seek our true refuge. What shall we take as our refuge?

In these three worlds, there is nothing else but Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho. Only this is our refuge.

Buddho – this is the virtue of the Buddha, the name of the Buddha. Dhammo – this is the name of the Dhamma. Saṅgho – this is the name of the noble Saṅgha. We must come to know this. Our refuge is only this. Where then are the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha? Hurry and look carefully together to know them. "Over there!" "Right here!" – but where exactly can you pin them down?

The Buddha's teaching leads to freedom from dukkha (suffering). He taught us to abandon evil and do good. By coming here, we are doing good – you should know this. Good and evil are not found anywhere else. Happiness and suffering are not found anywhere else. They are with ourselves, right here as we sit. No less, no greater – just the size of our own body: one cubit wide, one fathom long, one span thick. This is the whole domain of the religion.

title: Ajahn Funn: The problem lies with our attachments. What are you still holding onto at the moment? You don’t have to worry about the past…
content:
Focus on the Present Moment: No Need to Worry About Past or Future

The problem lies with our attachments. What are you still holding onto at the moment? You don’t have to worry about the past or the future. Focus in on the present moment to see if the mind is experiencing pleasure or pain. Is it dark or is it bright? Watch what’s going on. Is it experiencing pleasure or pain? This inner sensitivity is what you can depend on. No one else can create it for you. It has to arise within you.

So keep watching. Whatever sound you hear in the forest won’t harm you. I promise. You don’t have to worry. Just keep watch on your mind.

title: Ajahn Funn: You will see the self. The self is the one who knows: "this is hair, this is body hair, this is nails, this…
content:
The Self Is the Knower – The Knower Does Not Cease, Does Not Perish

You will see the self. The self is the one who knows: "this is hair, this is body hair, this is nails, this is teeth, this is skin." The self is the one who knows happiness, knows suffering, knows good, knows evil. That very one is the self. Gaze at it. Make it see for certain. That one is not anything – not hair, not body hair, not nails, not teeth, not skin. It is only the knower. The knower does not cease, does not disappear, does not break, does not perish, is not destroyed. When it is empty, it knows emptiness. When it is finished, it knows finished. But the knower itself never finishes. It has been that way from the beginningless past. If we are deluded and take the knower to mix and merge, to grasp something else, then that becomes the origin (samudaya), becomes existence (bhava), becomes birth (jāti). This is how it is. If we determine to know truly, then there is nothing, it is not anything. It is merely knowing. That is its nature. When birth occurs, it knows – but why would it need to be born? When old age occurs, it knows – why would it need to grow old? When sickness occurs, it knows – why would it need to be sick? When death occurs, it knows – why would it need to die? When delusion occurs, it knows – then why be deluded? Therefore it is said: "Buddha" – the one who knows.

title: Ajahn Funn: Where is this knowledge? We must look closely. It is not anywhere else. Opanayiko – it is to be brought inward. Paccattaṃ –…
content:
Without Knowledge (Buddha), Nothing Can Be Relied Upon – Like a Dead Person

Where is this knowledge? We must look closely. It is not anywhere else. Opanayiko – it is to be brought inward. Paccattaṃ – to be known only by oneself. So we look closely and hold onto that knowledge. When we have no knowledge, we cannot rely on a single thing in this world. We cannot rely on our own saṅkhārā body. We cannot rely on wealth, possessions, or material objects. We cannot rely on buildings and houses. We cannot rely on villagers, marketplaces, or the nation. We cannot rely on wealth, possessions, or material objects. We cannot rely on buildings and restaurants. We cannot rely on villagers or marketplaces. We cannot rely on the nation. If we have no Buddha – that is, no knowledge – then this is the case. But if we have knowledge, then we can rely on everything. We can rely on the saṅkhārā body. We can rely on buildings and restaurants. We can rely on villagers, marketplaces, and the nation.

Therefore we should all practice opanayiko – bringing it inward to see. Without Buddha, without knowledge, nothing can be relied upon. It is like a dead person, you see. A dead person has no knowledge. The mind and consciousness are gone. Only the elements remain, so nothing can be relied upon.

title: Ajahn Funn: What will the future be like? They say: just look. Want to run for office? Will you get it? They say: just look.…
content:
Sandiṭṭhiko: The Practitioner Knows for Themselves – Just Look at Your Own Mind

What will the future be like? They say: just look. Want to run for office? Will you get it? They say: just look. Will you get it or not? You will get it if your mind is upright, cool, calm, comfortable in heart. How could you not get it? If your mind is disturbed and distressed, then you won't get it. That's the way it is. This Dhamma is sandiṭṭhiko – to be seen for oneself by the practitioner, known for oneself. How could you not know your own mind? Will you get it or not? Good or not good? Will you be rich or not rich? Just look. Are you beautiful or not? Just look. When our mind is good, we have beauty and handsomeness. When the mind is not good, we are mean and ugly. Just look. Now, from now on, each person look at their own mind. It won't take long – maybe thirty minutes. Give it a try.

Being born as a human being is exceedingly difficult, and human life does not have much time.

Having been born to encounter the Buddha's Dhamma is counted as a supreme blessing.

The Buddha taught not to be heedless, to practice diligently.

Right view (sammādiṭṭhi) is the first important gateway. If you do not resolve and decide, you remain slow and hesitant because you are deluded by the manners and gestures of the mind.

title: Ajahn Funn: Now, samādhi – beautiful in the middle is samādhi. We make the mind steady and established. Now, is our mind established or not?…
content:
Samādhi: The Mind Established Like Still Water, Clear and Calm

Now, samādhi – beautiful in the middle is samādhi. We make the mind steady and established. Now, is our mind established or not? Does it lean somewhere? Where is it stuck? Where is it caught? We just say: samādhi is the mind established. Try to establish it: is it established or not? If it is established, what is that like? It does not lean toward love or hate, does not become deluded by forms, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, or any mental objects. When it is established, whatever arises, we cease it. Then it reaches samādhi, the mind established. When the mind is calm and established, it becomes clear. This is samatha kammaṭṭhāna – know samatha as making the mind calm internally.

When our mind is calm internally, it is like still water. Still water is clear. When clear, we see causes, see results, see merit and wholesomeness, see happiness, see suffering, see good, see evil. It is calm. This is our mind calm. Then when it is about to go out to the left or to the right, front or back, above or below, we know. So it is said to be established. This is focusing, establishing mindfulness right here. This is what we should know and understand further about the practice of samādhi.

title: Ajahn Funn: The Buddha taught us to be steadfast so that we may end demerit and kamma, end all misfortunes. The mind is samādhi, the…
content:
If the Mind Does Not Produce Bhava and Jāti, Then There Is No Birth

The Buddha taught us to be steadfast so that we may end demerit and kamma, end all misfortunes. The mind is samādhi, the mind is steadfast. When the mind is peaceful, all things are peaceful. If this mind does not go to produce bhava and jāti, who will go to produce them? When the mind does not produce them, then birth does not exist. Where would aging come from? When aging does not exist, where would sickness and disease come from? When sickness and disease do not exist, where would death come from? When death does not exist, where would birth come from? It is like this. This is how we wander in saṃsāra, dying and being reborn, being reborn and dying, dying and being reborn, for countless aeons and eons, for infinite time. If we look steadily at the mind, we see that it is we ourselves who produce bhava and jāti. If we stop, then it is the deathless, it is something permanent and true, not changeable. Not going to produce bhava and jāti. When there is no jāti (birth), then there is no jarā (aging). When there is no jarā, then there is no byādhi (sickness). When there is no byādhi, then there is no maraṇa (death). This is how it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: In the past, when they listened, they drew the teaching inwards to their own minds and hearts. Merit arose right then. The mind…
content:
Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho Are Our Refuge Within the Heart

In the past, when they listened, they drew the teaching inwards to their own minds and hearts. Merit arose right then. The mind became cool and refreshed, light and at ease. That is merit itself. Do we have it in our minds? Are we happy and at ease? Right now, as we are sitting here, look and see. Recollect: Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho. Recollect.

Where is Buddho? Where is Dhammo? Where is Saṅgho? This is our refuge and recollection, what we pay homage to, bow to, venerate. If we have no Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho, then we have no refuge. Having Buddho, Dhammo, Saṅgho is our refuge, our recollection, what we bow to and venerate. Draw it inwards. Where is Buddho? Is it not in our heart? Contemplate Buddho. Right now, what do you know? Do you know happiness or suffering? Do you know good or evil? Or do you know just neutral? Look at Buddho. Where is your mind abiding? Is it in the wind and air, or somewhere else? Is it with your children and grandchildren, with your home and possessions, or with your rice, belongings, money, and gold? Draw it inwards to yourself. One who knows the religion must draw it inwards, must know the root of the religion.

title: Ajahn Funn: If I keep explaining like this, there’s no end. To sum up, it all comes down to this body and mind. Focus, contemplate:…
content:
Transcending Suffering Means the Mind Does Not Suffer

If I keep explaining like this, there’s no end. To sum up, it all comes down to this body and mind. Focus, contemplate: good and evil, both external and internal, have been explained so that you know. Now, opanayiko – is it real or not? Let us all focus: where is it stuck? Where is it caught? Where is it not yet resolved? Focus right there. Do not send it forward, backward, left, right, above, below. Set it right at the middle, at that which knows. This is it. Whatever it is like, we keep correcting it there, keep purifying it there. That is what is meant by looking – not looking at anything else. Look at our own mind, look at our own becoming, look at our own refuge. Look so that you know. Whether the seat is good or not, we must know right here. Sanditthiko – the practitioner knows for themselves, sees for themselves. If we don’t know, others can tell us but we won’t know. This is how the practice is. From now on, whatever sound you hear, remind yourself: that thing is harmless, we need not be troubled. Make your mind… I will not explain further. Let us become calm. Each one calm down. Let go, make yourself comfortable. We want happiness and ease, so that it becomes our merit and our spiritual potential, so that we transcend suffering. We all want to transcend suffering – look: transcending suffering means our mind is not suffering. When our mind does not suffer, then we have transcended suffering. It is not about transcending in the sky or air. Look: if it is still suffering, it has not transcended suffering.
